# Introduction

"Do different penguin species differ in their overall physical characteristics, and does MANOVA provide additional insight compared with conducting separate univariate ANOVAs?"

# Data

The data was collected for research that was conducted as part of the Palmer Station, Antarctica, Long-Term Ecological Research program which was supported by grants through the National Science Foundation, Office of Polar Programs (NSF-OPP). Data was originally listed as three separate datasets within the Palmer Station Long-Term Ecological Research (PAL-LTER) data system and was combined into the single Palmer penguins dataset. Data were collected and made available by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station, Antarctica LTER, a member of the Long Term Ecological Research Network. The data used in this analysis is provided by @penguins. All analysis was performed in @R.

From the provided dataset I select for the three species of Antarctic penguins, Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo which will serve as the three species groups and the independent variable for my analysis. I will evaluate them based on the observed measurements of four physical characteristics bill length, bill depth, flipper length, and body mass which will be my dependent variables. Bill length, bill depth, and flipper length are recorded in units of millimeters (mm) and body mass was recorded in units of grams (g).

First we observe the dataset in @tbl-summary. At a glance, we can see that there are some similarities between the species. Bill depth, flipper length, and body mass of Adelie and Chinstrap penguins are more similar with each other than with Gentoo. However, Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins share a similar mean bill length. Additionally, note the smaller sample size of Chinstrap penguins. If we also have unequal covariance matrices, this may affect the reliability of our MANOVA results.

```{r, summary}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Summary Statistics of Key Variable Means and Sample Size by Species"

summary <- penguins %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_bill_length = mean(bill_length_mm),
    mean_bill_depth = mean(bill_depth_mm),
    mean_flipper_length = mean(flipper_length_mm),
    mean_body_mass = mean(body_mass_g)
  )

knitr::kable(
  summary %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 3))),
  caption = "Summary Statistics of Penguin Measurements",
  booktabs = TRUE
)
```

The data is further explored in @fig-vis which shows the distribution of the four physical measurements in the dataset. From the boxplot, we see that there are a few outliers which may affect our results. We also see some asymmetry in the body mass of Gentoo penguins and in the bill length of Chinstrap penguins.

```{r}
#| label: fig-vis
#| fig-cap: "Visualization of Key Variable Means and Sample Size by Species"
penguins_long <- penguins %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      bill_length_mm,
      bill_depth_mm,
      flipper_length_mm,
      body_mass_g
    ),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "measurement"
  )

ggplot(penguins_long,
       aes(x = species, y = measurement, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Body Measurements Across Penguin Species",
    x = "Penguin Species",
    y = "Measurement"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

Since we expect there to be some correlation between dependent variables, I calculate the correlation matrix and present the results in @tbl-correlation From the results, we see that bill length and bill depth are weakly negatively correlated (r = -0.235) and that flipper length and body mass are strongly correlated (r = 0.871). While flipper length and body mass are strongly correlated, there is no evidence of perfect multicollinearity.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-correlation
#| tbl-cap: "Correlation Matrix of Physical Measurements"
cor_matrix <- cor(
                  penguins[, 2:5],
                  use = "complete.obs"
              )

knitr::kable(
  round(cor_matrix, 3),
  caption = "Correlation Matrix of Penguin Measurements",
  digits = 3,
  booktabs = TRUE
)
```


# Methods

In order to investigate whether penguin species differ in their physical measurements I will consider four characteristics simultaneously: bill length, bill depth, flipper length, and body mass. First, I will start with four separate one-way ANOVAs tested on each of the four characteristics. The four one-way ANOVAs will test whether penguin species differ across bill length, bill depth, flipper length, and body mass simultaneously. Each ANOVA tests whether the mean of one dependent variable differs across the three species groups. The general one-way ANOVA model is $$Y_{ij} = \mu + \alpha_i + \epsilon_{ij} $$ where $Y_{ij}$ is the observed measurement for penguin $j$ for species $i$. $\mu$ is the overall population mean. $\alpha_i$ is the effect of the $i$-th species. $\epsilon_{ij}$ is the random error associated with each observation. This error tern is assumed to be independently and normally distributed with mean zero and variance $\epsilon_{ij} \sim N(0,\sigma^2)$. For ANOVA, we assume independence of observations, normality of residuals, and homogeneous population variance.


For each of the individual univariate ANOVAs, I will have a set of hypotheses for a total of four. My Null Hypothesis for each characteristic will be $$H_0: \mu_{Adelie}=\mu_{Chinstrap}=\mu_{Gentoo}$$ with an alternative hypothesis of $$ H_A: At \enspace least \enspace one \enspace species \enspace mean \enspace differs $$

With Anova, we can see which specific aspect variables differ since each variable gets its own
p-value. The limitation is that each ANOVA examines one outcome independently. This means we aren't directly testing whether penguin species affects the overall combination of physical characteristics. Additionally, with multiple tests, we inflate the risk of type 1 errors. Because of this, I will use MANOVA which considers all four dependent variables simultaneously. MANOVA tests whether the three penguin species have significantly different multivariate mean vectors; however, it does not identify which specific measurements differ.

The general one-way MANOVA model is $$\mathbf{Y}_{ij} = \mathbf{\mu} + \mathbf{\alpha}_i + \mathbf{\epsilon}_{ij} $$ where $\mathbf{Y}_{ij}$ is the vector of the four observed measurement for penjuin $j$ in species $i$. $\mathbf{\mu}$ is the overall multivariate population mean vector. $\mathbf{\alpha}_i$ is the multivariate effect of species $i$. $\mathbf{\epsilon}_{ij}$ is the vector of random errors. The $\mathbf{\epsilon}_{ij}$ are independent $N_4(0,\Sigma)$ where $\Sigma$ is the common covariance matrix.

Since MANOVA evaluates the combined mean vectors, we have the null hypothesis which states that all three species have equal population mean vectors $$H_0:\mu_{Adelie}=\mu_{Chinstrap}=\mu_{Gentoo}$$ and the alternative hypothesis $$ H_A: At \enspace least \enspace one \enspace mean \enspace vector \enspace differs$$

For MANOVA, we assume independence of observations, a common covariance matrix, and that each population is multivariate normal.

One assumption made when comparing two or more multivariate mean vectors is that the covariance matrices of the populations are the same. One test for equal covariance matrices is Box's M-test. The null hypothesis is that the covariance matrix for each of the populations are equal to each other and to the common covariance matrix. $$ H_0:\Sigma_1=\Sigma_2=\Sigma_3=\Sigma$$ The alternative hypothesis is that at least two of the covariance matrices are not equal. I will use this test to evaluate the common covariance matrix assumption at the end.

# Results

```{r}
# Four univariate ANOVA
anova_bill_length <- aov(bill_length_mm ~ species, data = penguins)
anova_bill_depth <- aov(bill_depth_mm ~ species, data = penguins)
anova_flipper <- aov(flipper_length_mm ~ species, data = penguins)
anova_body <- aov(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins)

#summary(anova_bill_length)
#summary(anova_bill_depth)
#summary(anova_flipper)
#summary(anova_body)

anova_models <- list(
  "Bill Length" = anova_bill_length,
  "Bill Depth" = anova_bill_depth,
  "Flipper Length" = anova_flipper,
  "Body Mass" = anova_body
)

anova_table <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(anova_models), function(variable) {

    result <- summary(anova_models[[variable]])[[1]]

    data.frame(
      Variable = variable,
      df = result[1, "Df"],
      F_statistic = result[1, "F value"],
      p_value = result[1, "Pr(>F)"]
    )
  })
) %>%
  mutate(
    F_statistic = round(F_statistic, 3),
    p_value_display = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3),
    Significance = case_when(
      p_value < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p_value < 0.01  ~ "**",
      p_value < 0.05  ~ "*",
      TRUE ~ ""
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    Variable,
    df,
    F_statistic,
    p_value_display,
    Significance
  )

knitr::kable(
  anova_table,
  col.names = c(
    "Dependent Variable",
    "Degrees of Freedom",
    "F-statistic",
    "P-value",
    "Significance"
  ),
  caption = "One-Way ANOVA Results by Penguin Species",
  booktabs = TRUE
)
```

If the p-value associated with Pillai's Trace is below 0.05, you reject the null hypothesis.

This indicates that the penguin species differ significantly in their combined physical characteristics.

```{r}
# Mulitivariate MANOVA
manova_model <- manova(
  cbind(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) ~ species,
  data = penguins
)

#summary(manova_model, test = "Pillai")

# Extract MANOVA results
manova_result <- summary(manova_model, test = "Pillai")$stats

manova_table <- data.frame(
  Test = "Pillai's Trace",
  Pillai = manova_result[1, "Pillai"],
  F_statistic = manova_result[1, "approx F"],
  df = manova_result[1, "num Df"],
  Residual_df = manova_result[1, "den Df"],
  p_value = manova_result[1, "Pr(>F)"]
) %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(Pillai, F_statistic), ~round(.x, 3)),
    p_value = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3),
    Significance = case_when(
      as.numeric(p_value) < 0.001 ~ "***",
      as.numeric(p_value) < 0.01 ~ "**",
      as.numeric(p_value) < 0.05 ~ "*",
      TRUE ~ ""
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  manova_table,
  caption = "MANOVA Results Using Pillai's Trace",
  col.names = c(
    "Test",
    "Pillai's Trace",
    "Approx. F",
    "Numerator df",
    "Denominator df",
    "P-value",
    "Significance"
  ),
  booktabs = TRUE
)
```

If the p-value associated with Pillai's Trace is below 0.05, you reject the null hypothesis.

This indicates that the penguin species differ significantly in their combined physical characteristics.

```{r}
# Extract follow-up ANOVA results
manova_aov <- summary.aov(manova_model)

manova_followup <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(manova_aov), function(variable) {

    result <- manova_aov[[variable]]

    data.frame(
      Variable = variable,
      df = result[1, "Df"],
      F_statistic = result[1, "F value"],
      p_value = result[1, "Pr(>F)"]
    )
  })
) %>%
  mutate(
    F_statistic = round(F_statistic, 3),
    p_value_display = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3),
    Significance = case_when(
      p_value < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p_value < 0.01 ~ "**",
      p_value < 0.05 ~ "*",
      TRUE ~ ""
    )
  ) %>%
  select(
    Variable,
    df,
    F_statistic,
    p_value_display,
    Significance
  )

knitr::kable(
  manova_followup,
  col.names = c(
    "Dependent Variable",
    "Degrees of Freedom",
    "F-statistic",
    "P-value",
    "Significance"
  ),
  caption = "Univariate Follow-up Tests from MANOVA",
  booktabs = TRUE
)
```

If the p-value associated with Pillai's Trace is below 0.05, you reject the null hypothesis.

This indicates that the penguin species differ significantly in their combined physical characteristics.

```{r}
# Box's M-test for equality of covariance matrices
box_M <- boxM(
     penguins[, c(
         "bill_length_mm",
         "bill_depth_mm",
         "flipper_length_mm",
         "body_mass_g"
     )],
     penguins$species
)

boxm_table <- data.frame(
  Test = "Box's M",
  Chi_Square = round(box_M$statistic, 3),
  df = box_M$parameter,
  p_value = format.pval(box_M$p.value, digits = 3),
  Significance = ifelse(
    box_M$p.value < 0.001, "***",
    ifelse(box_M$p.value < 0.01, "**",
           ifelse(box_M$p.value < 0.05, "*", ""))
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  boxm_table,
  col.names = c(
    "Test",
    "Chi-square",
    "Degrees of Freedom",
    "P-value",
    "Significance"
  ),
  caption = "Box's M Test for Homogeneity of Covariance Matrices",
  booktabs = TRUE
)
```



Box's M test was conducted to assess the homogeneity of variance-covariance matrices across penguin species. The test was statistically significant, χ²(20) = 76.795, p < 0.001, indicating evidence that the covariance matrices differ across species. Therefore, the assumption of homogeneous covariance matrices was not satisfied.
# Discussion



This case study demonstrates the advantages of multivariate data analysis by comparing separate univariate ANOVAs with MANOVA when examining physical differences among penguin species. While individual ANOVAs provide information about differences in specific physical measurements, MANOVA evaluates whether species differ across multiple characteristics simultaneously while accounting for relationships among the dependent variables. This provides a more comprehensive understanding of group differences and reduces the need to rely exclusively on multiple independent hypothesis tests. Therefore, multivariate analysis is particularly valuable when research questions involve several related outcome variables.
